extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy writers, radio disc jockeys, and TV writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for writing very short-form comedy (one-liners/lines to be spoken in ~10 seconds) with emphasis on word economy, punchline placement, delivery, and integrating jokes into television dialogue. Draws on radio 'talk over intro' training and its application to TV writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / work within tight time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: When you only have ten seconds you must select the right words and the right number of words, and you must put them in the right order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10 seconds is a long time; 18 seconds is an eternity. Treat short intros/slots as 'brevity boot camp'—write with an awareness of strict time limits and practice trimming. When you write a joke, go back: can you trim it? Is there one word that can replace three?

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language and word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the single best, often-shorter, word or concept to carry the joke; one word can replace three and increase impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for funnier words or concepts; prefer concise wording (one-syllable when possible) unless the joke absolutely requires a longer, precise 'four-dollar' word. Example guidance from radio writers: 'I would sometimes...look for ways to tighten the set-up without making it feel rushed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The punch line has to come right before the vocal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When talking over a song intro (or any strict slot), place the punch so it lands immediately before the music/vocal or the end of the available time so listeners hear the payoff. Timing of the punch relative to the ending cue is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery clarity and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rush your one-liner; delivery must be clear so the audience hears the punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You might squeeze a joke in if you rush, but if the audience doesn't hear it clearly they won't laugh. Learn delivery from live practice (radio): enunciate, control pace, and time beats so the line reads cleanly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pause and negative space
rubrics_metrics.description: Pauses are effective; you don't have to fill every available second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A seven-second joke with a well-placed pause may get a bigger laugh than talking for the whole ten seconds. Consider silence or pause as a deliberate comedic tool rather than wasted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual function: joke must serve story/action (for TV)
rubrics_metrics.description: In television, jokes often have two functions — to get a laugh and move the action forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On good shows characters rarely stop just to do a joke; jokes should be woven into conversations and situations as the story continues at pace. Tight construction means jokes advance character or plot as well as providing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train in constrained formats to build skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice writing under strict constraints — radio song intros, commercials, Twitter-sized jokes — to develop tightness and spontaneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radio 'talk over intro' work, live commercials, and short-form platforms force you to choose words quickly and develop delivery. These formats served as invaluable training grounds for many successful TV/late-night writers and hosts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision and ruthless editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always revisit jokes to tighten, replace words, and test alternate phrasings for maximum impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go back to each line and ask if a word can be removed or swapped for a funnier alternative. The author emphasizes returning to a joke and trimming: 'When you write a joke, go back. Can you trim it?'
